title: Number Patterns, Sequences and Estimation
objectives: Classify a sequence as arithmetic, geometric, interleaved or second-difference (quadratic) and predict its next terms
Use differences and ratios as systematic tests rather than guesswork
Anchor-and-correct awkward products and estimate magnitudes with powers of two and ten
Run sanity checks that catch order-of-magnitude errors before they cost marks
motivation: Pattern questions are the fastest points on a numerical test if you have a systematic move for each sequence type, and estimation is what saves you when the numbers are deliberately ugly. A trader who can see that 498 x 51 must be 'about 25,000, so the 2,539 option is a decoy' catches transcription errors that no spreadsheet warns about. This lesson builds both reflexes with verified arithmetic.

blocks.text: Three workhorse sequence types, and the tests that identify them

blocks.md: Most test sequences come from four families, each with a two-second diagnostic. **Arithmetic**: consecutive differences are constant (each term adds a fixed amount). **Geometric**: consecutive ratios are constant (each term multiplies by a fixed factor). **Interleaved**: two or more alternating subsequences, each with its own simple rule. **Second-difference**: the first differences are not constant, but their *differences* are, a signature of a quadratic rule. Always run the tests in this order: differences first (cheap), ratios second, then split the sequence into odd and even positions, then take second differences.

blocks.title: Worked: 3, 7, 13, 21, 31, ...
items: First differences: $4, 6, 8, 10$ - not constant, so not arithmetic.
Second differences: $2, 2, 2$ - constant. This is the quadratic signature.
Extrapolate: the next first difference is $10 + 2 = 12$, so the next term is $31 + 12 = 43$.
Extra credit: constant second difference 2 means the rule is quadratic; here the terms are $n^2 + n + 1$, which reproduces all five terms (try $n = 1..5$).

blocks.md: The other families are quicker. Geometric: 5, 15, 45, 135 has ratios $3, 3, 3$, so the next term is $135 \times 3 = 405$. Interleaved: 2, 9, 4, 12, 6, 15 splits into odd positions $2, 4, 6$ (add 2) and even positions $9, 12, 15$ (add 3); the next term is position 7, so it belongs to the first subsequence: $8$. Fibonacci-style: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 has each term the sum of the previous two, so the next is $13 + 21 = 34$. When a sequence resists all four tests, check the rule 'multiply then add a constant': 3, 7, 15, 31 is $\times 2 + 1$ each time.

blocks.text: Estimation: make the numbers friendly, then correct

blocks.md: The **anchor-and-correct** method turns ugly products into friendly ones plus a small adjustment. For $7 \times 493$: anchor on $7 \times 500 = 3500$, then correct by $7 \times 7 = 49$ downward, giving $3451$ - exact, not approximate. For $498 \times 51$: the anchor $500 \times 50 = 25000$ tells you the answer is about 25,000 (exact: $25398$), which is enough to eliminate decoy options before you commit to precise arithmetic. In multiple-choice settings, estimate first and match orders of magnitude; only then do the exact computation for the surviving option.

Magnitude fluency relies on two reference facts: $2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$, so roughly ten doublings make a thousand times, and doubling growth always overtakes polynomial growth eventually. The chart below shows $2^x$ against $x^2$: they tie at $x = 4$ ($16 = 16$), and by $x = 5$ the exponential has pulled ahead ($32$ vs $25$) and never looks back.

blocks.caption: Doubling versus squaring: tied at $x = 4$, exponential ahead from $x = 5$ onward, the visual basis of every 'eventually dominates' estimation.

blocks.md: Percent-fraction fluency keeps estimates honest: 17% of 400 is $0.17 \times 400 = 68$, but the fast route is $10\% + 5\% + 2\% = 40 + 20 + 8 = 68$. And when a problem spans units (seconds to hours, bytes to gigabytes), carry the units through the estimate, catching a factor of $10^3$ error is exactly what estimation is for.

blocks.title: Companion practice: the Mental Math page
blocks.md: The platform's Mental Math page runs timed drills on friendly-number products, doubling chains and percent breakdowns, the same patterns as anchor-and-correct. A short warm-up there before practice sets trains the estimation reflex until it is automatic.

guidedExercise.prompt: Find the next term of the sequence 4, 9, 19, 39, 79, ... using two different methods, and state which family the sequence belongs to.
hints: Check the ratio between consecutive terms as well.
Try the rule 'multiply then add a constant'.
guidedExercise.solution: Method 1 (differences): first differences are $5, 10, 20, 40$ - each doubles, so the next difference is $80$ and the next term is $79 + 80 = 159$. Method 2 (recurrence): each term is twice the previous plus one ($4 \times 2 + 1 = 9$, $9 \times 2 + 1 = 19$, ...), so the next term is $79 \times 2 + 1 = 159$. Both routes agree on **159**; the sequence is geometric in its differences (a 'multiply-then-add' recurrence), which is why neither the plain arithmetic nor the plain geometric test fits.

independentExercise.prompt: A market-data feed delivers 3,000 messages per second and runs for an 8-hour trading session. (a) Estimate the number of messages per session, stating the seconds-per-hour conversion you used. (b) Each message carries 250 bytes; estimate the total data volume in gigabytes for one session. (c) Give one sanity check that would catch a factor-of-1000 error in (b).
hints: A gigabyte is $10^9$ bytes; check the final power of ten.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $3600 \times 8 = 28{,}800$ seconds; messages $= 3000 \times 28800 = 86{,}400{,}000 = 8.64 \times 10^7$ - about **86.4 million messages**. (b) Bytes $= 8.64 \times 10^7 \times 250 = 2.16 \times 10^{10} = 21.6 \times 10^9$, i.e. **21.6 GB**. (c) Sanity check: 3,000 messages per second is 3 million per thousand seconds, so an 8-hour day (~30 thousand seconds) must give tens of millions of messages, a result in billions of *messages* or gigabytes of *messages* would signal a slip from $10^7$ to $10^{10}$.

commonMistakes: Assuming a sequence is arithmetic because the first two differences look close: 4, 6, 8, 10 is not constant, only the second differences are.
Multiplying when the rule adds (or adding when the rule multiplies): run the difference test and the ratio test deliberately, not by vibe.
Anchoring in the wrong direction: $7 \times 493 = 3500 - 49$, not $3500 + 49$; the correction is 7 times how far 493 is below 500.
Estimating without units: mixing seconds/minutes or bytes/gigabytes silently shifts the answer by factors of 60 or 1000.
Reporting an interpolated term as the 'next term' in interleaved sequences, always check which subsequence the next position belongs to.
realWorldApplication: Capacity planning is estimation with stakes: engineers sanity-check message rates, storage and bandwidth with exactly these anchor-and-correct moves before any precise calculation, because a factor-of-1000 error found on paper costs nothing.
quantFinanceApplication: Market-data contracts bill by message counts in the tens of millions per day, and sequence fluency shows up in tick-data work: recognising doubling growth (2^10 ~ 10^3) lets you estimate when a feed doubles its storage bill long before the invoice arrives.
summary: Diagnostic order for sequences: differences, then ratios, then odd/even interleaving, then second differences; constant second differences mean a quadratic rule.
Multiply-then-add recurrences (e.g. each term = 2 x previous + 1) defeat all three simple tests, check them when the standard tests fail.
Anchor-and-correct: round to friendly numbers, then correct by the exact error (7 x 493 = 3500, 49 = 3451).
$2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$: ten doublings are a thousandfold, and exponentials overtake polynomials within a few steps.
Estimation is a verification tool: establish the magnitude first, then do exact arithmetic only for the plausible answer.

quiz.prompt: What is the next term of 3, 7, 13, 21, 31, ...?
quiz.explanation: First differences are 4, 6, 8, 10 (increasing by 2), so the next difference is 12 and the next term is $31 + 12 = 43$.

quiz.prompt: What is the next term of 5, 15, 45, 135, ...?
quiz.explanation: Consecutive ratios are constantly 3, so the next term is $135 \times 3 = 405$.

quiz.prompt: What is the next term of 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...?
quiz.explanation: Each term is the sum of the two before it: $13 + 21 = 34$. (Decoys: 33 and 35 come from adding only one term; 42 doubles the wrong quantity.)

quiz.prompt: Anchor on $500 \times 50$ to estimate, then compute exactly: $498 \times 51 = ?$
quiz.explanation: Anchor $500 \times 50 = 25000$. Exactly: $498 \times 51 = 498 \times 50 + 498 = 24900 + 498 = 25398$ - close to the anchor, which is why the anchor is useful for eliminating implausible options first.

quiz.prompt: Select every statement about sequences that is TRUE.
options: Constant first differences mean the rule is arithmetic
Constant second differences mean the rule is quadratic
Constant ratios between consecutive terms mean the rule is geometric
Any sequence with alternating positive and negative terms must be geometric
quiz.explanation: The first three are the standard diagnostic signatures. The fourth is false: alternation can come from many rules (e.g. interleaved subsequences, or 'multiply by -2 then add 3'), sign pattern alone identifies nothing.

quiz.prompt: A feed runs at 3,000 messages per second for 8 hours. How many million messages is that (to one decimal place)?
quiz.explanation: $3600 \times 8 = 28800$ seconds; $3000 \times 28800 = 86{,}400{,}000 = 86.4$ million. Sanity check: 3 thousand per second for ~30 thousand seconds gives tens of millions.

flashcards.back: Differences (arithmetic) -> ratios (geometric) -> odd/even subsequences (interleaved) -> second differences (quadratic). If all fail, try 'multiply then add a constant'.
A quadratic rule. E.g. 3, 7, 13, 21, 31 has second differences of 2 and matches $n^2 + n + 1$.
Round to friendly numbers, multiply, then correct by the exact error: $7 \times 493 = 7 \times 500 - 7 \times 7 = 3500 - 49 = 3451$.
$2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3$ (ten doublings = a thousandfold) and a 25% rise then 25% fall = 0.9375. Powers of 2 sit near powers of 10.
